Vatican City. The world's smallest independent state and the spiritual and administrative center of the Roman Catholic Church. Located entirely within Rome on just 0.44 square kilometers, Vatican City is bounded by the Leonine Walls and is the residence of the Pope, head of the Catholic Church.

Vatican City became a sovereign city-state in 1929 through the Lateran Treaty signed between the Holy See and Mussolini's fascist Italy, resolving decades of papal-Italian tension that had accumulated since Italian unification in 1870.

The Pope is the absolute sovereign of Vatican City, exercising executive, legislative, and judicial authority, though administrative functions are typically delegated to a governing body.

St. Peter's Basilica, the largest church in Christendom and the principal church of the Catholic Church, stands in Vatican City and is one of the Renaissance's greatest architectural achievements.

Vatican City houses the Roman Curia, the administrative and judicial apparatus of the Catholic Church, with numerous offices, departments, and councils that govern Church affairs worldwide.

The Vatican Archives and Library contain centuries of historical documents, manuscripts, and records, making the Vatican a major repository of Western religious and political history.

A small Swiss Guard, a corps of Swiss mercenary soldiers dating to the sixteenth century, protects the Pope. They are distinctive for their colorful Renaissance-era uniforms.

Vatican City maintains its own independence as a nation-state in subtle but real ways. It issues its own stamps and coins, maintains a radio station, and is the only state with Latin as an official language, preserving Latin liturgy and scholarly tradition. At the United Nations, Vatican City holds permanent observer status, allowing it to participate in international diplomacy and advocate for Catholic social teaching.

As the seat of Catholic Church authority, Vatican City stands at the heart of Christianity's largest denomination. The Counter-Reformation, the religious reform movement centered in Rome, reshaped the Church from this city. The Renaissance, the artistic and cultural movement, produced Vatican's greatest architectural and artistic treasures.
